newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude drifts to lower end led by heating oil.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude drifts to lower end led by heating oil.

text.p: NYMEX crude drifted to a lower end Thursday in lacklustre trade, led by losses in heating oil following forecasts of above normal temperatures next week in the U.S. Northeast.
The forecasts extend what has been a relatively mild winter in the region thus far.
Prompt gasoline, on the other hand, ended higher on short covering ahead of the March expiry in refined products on Friday. The back months in gasoline were weaker.
April crude settled off 22 cents off at $20.89 a barrel, just above its session low of $20.84.
March heating oil ended off 0.65 cent at 56.03 cents a gallon while March gasoline finished up 0.41 cent at 62.67 cents a gallon.
"It looks like heating oil led the move. The weather seems to continue above normal, so we should be in this downtrend for the next month," said Mike De Luca, trader with Prudential Securities.

The National Weather Service and independent forecaster Weather Services Corp called for temperatures to average above normal into next week in the key heating oil market of the northeastern United States.
Besides poor heating oil demand, heavy refinery maintenance has cut crude usage when gasoline demand is in a seasonal trough before rising in the spring and summer.
The downtrend in oil prices has already lasted for about a month, lopping 20 percent off crude and heating oil prices.

Technically oil prices had what is called an "inside day" Thursday, reflecting price action that falls within the previous day's range. With prices failing to make lower lows, chartists said the oil complex may be bottoming.
Dealers said the day's tighter price range was really due to a lack of market momentum amid neutral news.
Workers who process export documents for oil shipments in Nigeria decided to hold off striking Friday pending a union meeting Monday.

Meanwhile, U.N. sources said Thursday that the latest crude contract approved by U.N.-appointed overseers under the oil-for-food accord puts Iraq at the monetary cap of $1 billion for the first 90-day period of the six-month deal.
But, dealers shrugged off the news since the market has anticipated the oil sales since the accord was approved last December.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
